design_detail: Open intravenous pharmacokinetic study, without placebo or randomization, in 4 men who used cocaine frequently: 100 mg in 3 men (participants W, X and Y) and 200 mg in 2 (W and Z) in separate sessions, so that one man (W) received both doses; each dose infused over about 1.5 to 3 minutes; blood drawn from the other arm (venous by implication; the paper does not say) every 5 to 60 minutes for 3 to 6 hours and the plasma assayed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. One- or two-exponential curves were fitted to each session, and half-life, volume of distribution, clearance and back-extrapolated initial concentration were regressed on dose in mg/kg across the 5 sessions. A sixth session in Z (100 mg followed by a second 100 mg 30 minutes later) appears only in the Results (Fig. 5). The paper adds a reanalysis of published mean plasma curves from other laboratories (intravenous and intranasal doses in 10 volunteers, Javaid et al., 1978b; oral and intranasal topical doses in 4 people, Van Dyke et al., 1978) and a reinterpretation of a coca-chewing study (Holmstedt et al., 1979). Order: not randomized or counterbalanced (the order of W's two sessions is not stated; Z's 200 mg session came before his repeated-dose session). Blinding: none reported. Participants: men with documented frequent cocaine use; their route of use and whether they were seeking treatment are not stated.
can_establish: Plasma cocaine concentrations, in blood drawn from the arm opposite the infusion, over 3 to 6 hours after single intravenous doses of 100 and 200 mg in four men who used cocaine frequently, with descriptive half-life, volume and clearance estimates for these five sessions, including one within-person comparison of the two doses.
cannot_establish: A general relationship between dose and half-life or clearance (five sessions in four men, mostly between-person, with no tests or intervals); bioavailability or absorption rate by any route other than intravenous (those figures are reanalyses of other laboratories' averaged data); the risk of accumulation with repeated use (one repeated-dose session in one man); any effect of the drug (none is reported); or anything about coca chewing, which was not studied.

sample.recruitment: Not stated. Four male volunteers with documented histories of frequent cocaine self-administration; the paper does not say how they were recruited or where the sessions took place. The authors were at the Division of Research of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, Rockville, and the Department of Psychiatry of New York Medical College (pp. 353, 354).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Frequent self-administration of cocaine during the preceding 6 months, by the authors' account at doses comparable to those given in the study; at least 48 hours without cocaine before each session; all met FDA requirements for participation in experimental studies with cocaine (the requirements are not described) and signed an informed consent. No other criteria, medical screening results or ethics-committee approval are reported (p. 354).
sample.demographics: Four men; body weights 68 kg (W), 95 kg (X), 58 kg (Y) and 86 kg (Z) (Table 1, p. 357). Age, ethnicity, the route of their own cocaine use, other drug use and treatment status are not reported.
sample.attrition: None reported; all five single-dose sessions described in the Methods appear in Table 1 (p. 357).
sample.selection_effects: Four men only, selected for frequent use at doses near those studied; their route of use, health and treatment status are unknown. Because doses were fixed in mg and bodies differed in weight, and only one man received both doses, the dose comparison is largely a comparison between people: the 200 mg sessions were in the men weighing 68 and 86 kg, the 100 mg sessions in men weighing 58 to 95 kg.

exposure.measurement: Drug given intravenously in the laboratory and measured in plasma from blood drawn from the other arm, by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (Finnigan 1015 or 3200, chemical ionization, selected-ion monitoring) with trideuterated cocaine as internal standard; standard curves from 2 to 500 ng/ml were prepared in each participant's pre-dose plasma with every batch and accepted if the correlation exceeded 0.980; blood was collected into tubes with sodium fluoride, which the authors report prevented hydrolysis in the sample on repeat analysis over one year (pp. 353–355). No precision, accuracy, limit of quantification or dilution procedure is reported. Participants' own cocaine use is known only from their documented histories (p. 354).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: cocaine 100 mg (3 men) or 200 mg (2 men), dissolved in 1.5 ml and infused intravenously over about 1.5 to 3 minutes, one dose per session (p. 354). In mg/kg the five sessions were 1.05 (X), 1.47 (W), 1.72 (Y), 2.33 (Z) and 2.94 (W) (editors' calculation from the weights in Table 1, p. 357; the paper gives the range as 1.05 to 2.94 mg/kg, p. 361). In one further session Z received 100 mg followed by a second 100 mg 30 minutes later (p. 363). Whether the doses are expressed as salt or base is not stated, nor the source and purity of the drug given: the 98% purity stated under Chemical analysis concerns the cocaine hydrochloride and deuterated cocaine obtained from NIDA, and the paper does not say whether the same material was given to participants (p. 354). The reanalysed literature data concern 32 mg intravenous and 96 mg intranasal doses (Javaid et al., 1978b) and 2 mg/kg oral and intranasal topical doses (Van Dyke et al., 1978) (pp. 356, 358).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: no information on the participants' alcohol, tobacco or other drug use.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 48 hours without cocaine before each session, by the authors' statement; how this was verified is not reported, and no pre-dose cocaine concentrations are printed (p. 354).

comparison.controls: None: no placebo session and no comparison group. The dose comparison is between sessions (three at 100 mg, two at 200 mg) and is within one person only for W. The non-intravenous estimates compare other laboratories' published mean curves with intravenous mean curves, in one case from a different laboratory (p. 361).
comparison.matching: Not applicable; doses are expressed per kg body weight in the regressions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions as such; but between-person differences in metabolism, body composition and recent use, which could produce the same pattern as dose dependence when most comparisons are between people, were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Venous plasma cocaine by the assay described; curves fitted by nonlinear regression to one or two exponentials with each point weighted by 1/C²; terminal half-life (0.693/β), absorption half-life (0.693/α), total clearance (dose/AUC), volume of distribution (dose/(β·AUC)), back-extrapolated initial concentration (B, or A + B for a two-exponential fit) and bioavailability from dose-normalized AUC ratios (eqns 1–7, pp. 355–356); linear and exponential regressions of these parameters on dose in mg/kg (pp. 361–362).
outcomes.validity_norms: In-house assay with per-batch calibration; no validation statistics are reported. The model-based quantities (AUC, clearance, initial concentration) depend on the model chosen for each curve.
outcomes.operationalization: Dose dependence is a correlation across sessions between dose per kg and a fitted parameter. Accumulation is a measured concentration 5 minutes after a second dose compared with the sum of two concentrations from the first dose. No effects, harms or vital-sign data are reported, although vital signs were monitored throughout (p. 354).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable in the usual sense: four parameters (half-life, volume of distribution, clearance, initial concentration) are related to dose, but no P values, confidence intervals or tests are reported for any of them; the one statement of non-significance (p. 359) is judged from coefficients of variation without a test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the outcomes are assay values and fitted parameters.

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals or P values are reported. Terminal half-life after 100 mg: 51.5 (W), 40.3 (X) and 47.2 min (Y); after 200 mg: 82.3 (W) and 78.9 min (Z). Volume of distribution 116, 179, 87.8, 83.7 and 140 L (1.71, 1.88, 1.51, 1.23 and 1.63 L/kg). Clearance 93.9, 185, 77.3, 42.3 and 73.6 L/h (1.38, 1.95, 1.33, 0.62 and 0.86 L/h per kg) (Table 3, p. 360). Regressions across the 5 sessions: half-life (min) = 13.5 + 24.5 × dose (mg/kg), r = 0.946; clearance (L/kg per h) = 2.51 − 0.67 × dose, r = −0.973; volume of distribution r = −0.89 (p. 361; Figs 2–3, p. 362). Editors' calculation: the regressions reproduce from Table 3 (half-life 13.4 + 24.5 × dose, r = 0.945; clearance r = −0.973; volume r = −0.890), and with n = 5 the 95% interval for r = 0.946 runs from about 0.39 to 0.997 (Fisher z), treating W's two sessions as independent. Within W, half-life rose by 60%, volume of distribution fell by 28% and clearance by 55% from 100 to 200 mg (p. 363). Intranasal bioavailability from the reanalysis of Javaid et al. (1978b): 0.6 (Table 3, p. 360; p. 361).
analysis.covariates: None; dose is expressed per kg body weight.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or pre-specified analysis is mentioned; the model for each curve (one or two exponentials) and the weighting were chosen by goodness of fit (pp. 355, 358).
analysis.selective_reporting: The repeated-dose session in Z is not in the Methods; its data appear only in Fig. 5 and as three values in the text (pp. 362–363). Vital signs were monitored throughout (p. 354) but none are reported. The literature datasets were selected with stated reasons: only the high-dose data of Javaid et al. were used, and the data of Kogan et al. (1977) were set aside (pp. 356–357).
analysis.power: Not reported; five sessions in four men, with the within-person comparison resting on one man.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four men who used cocaine frequently, plasma cocaine after a 100 mg intravenous infusion fell from 682–1005 ng/ml at 5 minutes with terminal half-lives of 40–52 minutes, and after 200 mg from 2530–3868 ng/ml with half-lives of 79–82 minutes and about half the clearance per kg; the one man given both doses showed the same pattern. One repeated-dose session in one man gave 6990 ng/ml 5 minutes after a second 100 mg dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary (p. 353) presents as general results equations for half-life and clearance as functions of dose over 1 to 3 mg/kg, absorption half-lives of about 8 minutes for gastrointestinal and intranasal absorption and an intranasal bioavailability of about 60%, and concludes that modern routes of use could lead to unexpected accumulation of cocaine in blood while coca chewing is unlikely to. The Conclusions call the findings tentative because of the small number of participants and the averaged literature data (p. 363), yet state that the half-life "must be expressed in terms of the linear equation" (p. 363) and that the dose dependence strongly suggests saturation of metabolism at the doses studied (p. 364), with no metabolite data. The bioavailability and absorption figures are not measurements from this study: they come from refitting other laboratories' averaged curves, with an intranasal absorption rate constant whose coefficient of variation was 72% (Table 2, p. 358), intranasal sampling only to 1.5 hours (p. 359) and an assumed 20-minute lag for the oral data (p. 358). The accumulation warning rests on one session in one man (p. 363) and on a jump in initial concentration that depends on a single model-based value (pp. 361–362, 364). The coca-chewing conclusion rests on another group's data and an uncalculated projection to a 30 g quid (pp. 364–365).

timeline.event: Kogan et al.: 100 mg intravenously in three people, reported with a 2.8-hour terminal phase from a multiexponential fit; refitted here as a single exponential and set aside because that assay's precision and accuracy were shown only down to 250 ng/ml (pp. 356–357). Richard Resnick is an author of both papers (reference list, p. 365).

Javaid et al. (1978b): 16 and 32 mg intravenously and 16, 64 and 96 mg intranasally in the same 10 volunteers, assayed without an internal standard; only the 32 mg intravenous and 96 mg intranasal mean curves were reanalysed here, giving the 60% intranasal bioavailability (pp. 356, 361).
Van Dyke et al.: 2 mg/kg orally and by intranasal topical application in the same four people; mean curves reanalysed here (pp. 356, 358).
Wilkinson, Van Dyke et al.: follow-up oral and intranasal kinetic study reporting mean terminal half-lives of 75 and 48 minutes (the routes are assigned inconsistently in this paper's text, p. 359).

Evans et al.: 16 and 32 mg intravenously over 10 seconds with simultaneous radial-artery and venous sampling from 5 seconds into the injection; venous concentrations peaked about 4 minutes after injection, arterial concentrations at 15 seconds at about ten times the venous peak. Half-life and clearance were not estimated.

replication.where_it_stands: An early intravenous pharmacokinetic study whose half-lives of 40–82 minutes come from curves fitted to arm blood samples taken from 5 minutes onward in five sessions. Its dose dependence of half-life and clearance, and its 60% intranasal bioavailability, were not re-tested in the sources read for this card; later pharmacokinetic studies on the cocaine list (for example Jeffcoat et al., 1989, cited by Evans et al., 1996) should be read before either figure is used on its own. The arterial data of Evans et al. (1996) show that in the first minutes after an intravenous dose venous concentrations are far below arterial concentrations, so the arm samples analysed here (venous by implication) miss the early arterial peak.

funding.funder: Not reported: the paper has no funding statement. The cocaine hydrochloride and deuterated cocaine used in the chemical analysis were obtained from NIDA (p. 354); the acknowledgements name individuals only (Dr. Robert Willette, Dr. Vojtech Licko and Maria Amelia Josefina Burgos, p. 365).
funding.affiliations_note: Barnett and Hawks: Division of Research, National Institute on Drug Abuse, Rockville, MD; Resnick: New York Medical College, Department of Psychiatry (p. 353). Resnick is also an author of Kogan et al. (1977), the dataset this paper sets aside (p. 365). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: The same people given several intravenous doses across the range in randomized order, with an assay validated over the full concentration range (or a documented dilution step), dense early sampling, metabolite measurement and non-compartmental estimates, would show whether cocaine clearance falls with dose. For intranasal bioavailability: intranasal and intravenous doses in the same people, measured with one validated assay and sampled long enough to define the terminal phase.

domains.domain: Randomization process (allocation and order of the dose conditions)
domains.note: Doses were neither randomized nor counterbalanced: three men received 100 mg and two received 200 mg, one man (W) both, and the order of his two sessions is not stated. The dose comparison is therefore mostly between people whose weights (58–95 kg) and other characteristics differ (pp. 354, 357).

Open administration without placebo; infusion time varied from about 1.5 to 3 minutes, which affects early concentrations and the back-extrapolated initial values; the repeated-dose session in Z is not part of the described protocol; sampling times differed between sessions (Table 1, p. 357). Blinding matters little for assay outcomes.

All five single-dose sessions are tabulated, but late values printed as 0 (X at 240, 300 and 360 minutes; Y at 360 minutes) imply concentrations below the assay's range, and how they entered the 1/C²-weighted fits is not stated; the repeated-dose session is shown only in a figure.

Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry with a deuterated internal standard is objective, but calibration covered 2–500 ng/ml while the first values after 100 mg and most values in the first hour after 200 mg exceeded 500 ng/ml (up to 3868 ng/ml in Table 1 and 6990 ng/ml in the repeated-dose session), with no dilution, precision or accuracy data. These early values determine the fitted intercepts, AUC, clearance and initial concentrations.

No protocol. The model for each curve was chosen by fit; the only two-exponential fit (W, 200 mg) supplies both the longest half-life and the outlying initial concentration behind the claimed threshold, and the authors state that a single exponential would give a slightly larger β, that is a shorter half-life (p. 358). Literature datasets were selected with stated reasons.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The assay values are objective, but the paper's main conclusion, that half-life and clearance depend on dose, rests on five open sessions in four men in which dose was not randomized and was largely confounded with the person, with one within-person pair, no tests or intervals, and early concentrations above the calibrated range. The source can be cited for the plasma concentrations measured over up to 6 hours after 100 mg and 200 mg of intravenous cocaine in these four men, and for half-lives of 40–52 minutes after 100 mg and 79–82 minutes after 200 mg in these sessions. It cannot be cited for a general dose–half-life or dose–clearance equation, for intranasal bioavailability or absorption rates as measured values (they are reanalyses of other laboratories' averaged data), for accumulation with repeated use (one session in one man), or for any statement about coca chewing.

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: four men with documented frequent cocaine self-administration in the preceding 6 months received cocaine by intravenous infusion over about 1.5 to 3 minutes, after at least 48 hours without cocaine: 100 mg in three men and 200 mg in two, one man receiving both in separate sessions; blood (10 ml) was drawn from the other arm every 5 to 60 minutes over 3 to 6 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Clinical protocol, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 354, the 3rd continuing on p. 355)

key_findings.finding: The first sample, 5 minutes after the infusion, held the highest measured concentration in every session: 921, 682 and 1005 ng/ml after 100 mg (W, X, Y) and 3868 and 2530 ng/ml after 200 mg (W, Z). At 60 minutes the values were 430, 170 and 477 ng/ml after 100 mg and 1222 and 990 ng/ml after 200 mg. Doses per kg, by the editors' calculation from the weights in Table 1 (68, 95, 58 and 86 kg): 1.47, 1.05 and 1.72 mg/kg at 100 mg; 2.94 and 2.33 mg/kg at 200 mg.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Intravenous data, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Table 1 shows two rises during the decline (W at 100 mg: 352 ng/ml at 45 minutes, then 430 at 60; X: 254 at 30 minutes, then 290 at 45) that the text does not discuss. The machine-read text layer misreads X's weight; the printed page shows 95 kg.

key_findings.finding: Terminal half-lives were 51.5 (W), 40.3 (X) and 47.2 minutes (Y) after 100 mg, and 82.3 (W) and 78.9 minutes (Z) after 200 mg.
key_findings.note: The machine-read text layer of this page gives 41.2 for Y; the printed page shows 47.2, which matches 0.693/β from Table 2 (0.693/0.0147 = 47.1, editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Volume of distribution was 84 to 179 L (1.23 to 1.88 L/kg); clearance was 1.38, 1.95 and 1.33 L/h per kg in the three 100 mg sessions and 0.62 and 0.86 L/h per kg in the two 200 mg sessions, about half, as the authors put it.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Pharmacokinetic parameters, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Across the five sessions, terminal half-life rose with dose (half-life in minutes = 13.5 + 24.5 × dose in mg/kg, r = 0.946) and clearance fell (clearance in L/kg per hour = 2.51 − 0.67 × dose, r = −0.973); volume of distribution fell more weakly (r = −0.89). From the equations the authors derive half-lives of 38 and 87 minutes and clearances of 1.8 and 0.5 L/kg per hour at 1 and 3 mg/kg.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Dose dependence, 1st paragraph (p. 361); Figs 2 and 3 (p. 362); Conclusions, 2nd paragraph (pp. 363–364)
key_findings.note: Five sessions in four men, one man contributing two; no P values or intervals. Editors' calculation: the equations reproduce from Table 3 (13.4 + 24.5 × dose, r = 0.945), and the 95% interval for r = 0.946 with n = 5 is about 0.39 to 0.997 (Fisher z). The values at 1 and 3 mg/kg lie at or just outside the studied range of 1.05 to 2.94 mg/kg.

key_findings.finding: In the one man given both doses (W), going from 100 to 200 mg (1.47 to 2.95 mg/kg) lengthened the half-life by 60% (51.5 to 82.3 minutes) and lowered volume of distribution by 28% and clearance by 55%.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 360); Results and discussion › Dose dependence, 1st paragraph (begins p. 361; this passage pp. 362–363)
key_findings.note: The same 200 mg dose is given as 2.94 mg/kg on p. 361 and 2.95 mg/kg on p. 363. This is the only within-person dose comparison, and W's 200 mg curve is the only one fitted with two exponentials.

key_findings.finding: Back-extrapolated initial concentration rose linearly with dose from 1.1 to 2.3 mg/kg (initial concentration = −137 + 691 × dose, r = 0.987), but the value at 2.9 mg/kg was 140% above that line; an exponential fit over the whole range (185 × e^dose, r = 0.969) still underestimated it by 33%. The authors read this as a threshold effect between 2.3 and 2.9 mg/kg.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Dose dependence, 1st paragraph (pp. 361–362); Fig. 4 (p. 362)
key_findings.note: The value at 2.9 mg/kg (4479 ng/ml, A + B from Table 2, editors' sum) is the only intercept from a two-exponential fit; the authors acknowledge it could be described as a computational artefact before arguing from Fig. 5 that it is reasonable (p. 364). See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: In one further session, Z received 100 mg followed by a second 100 mg 30 minutes later: the concentration 5 minutes after the second dose was 6990 ng/ml, against a prediction of the sum of the first dose's 5-minute (820 ng/ml) and 30-minute (554 ng/ml) values, which the authors describe as 400% above the prediction; the terminal half-life was 94.9 minutes, against 78.9 minutes after a single 200 mg dose in the same man.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Dose dependence, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 5 (p. 362)
key_findings.note: One session in one man, not described in the Methods; its data appear only in Fig. 5, whose legend does not say which symbols belong to which session (the triangles match the values for Z at 200 mg in Table 1). Editors' calculation: the predicted value is 1374 ng/ml and the measured value about five times that; read from Fig. 5 (editors, approximate), a second value of about 6000 ng/ml follows at about 40 minutes.

key_findings.finding: An intranasal bioavailability of about 0.6 (60%) was derived by refitting the mean plasma curves published by Javaid et al. (1978b) for 32 mg intravenous and 96 mg intranasal doses in the same 10 volunteers; the intranasal absorption half-life was 8.4 minutes, but the absorption rate constant had a coefficient of variation of 72%, and the authors judge the intranasal estimates poor because sampling in that study ran only to 1.5 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and Results and discussion › Literature data, 1st paragraph (p. 358); Pharmacokinetic parameters, 1st paragraph (p. 359) and 5th paragraph (p. 361); Table 3 (p. 360)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the Table 2 constants: about 56% of the intranasal AUC lies beyond the last sample at 90 minutes and is extrapolated from a terminal rate constant with a coefficient of variation of 38%. The calculation also assumes equal clearance at the two doses compared (eqn 6, pp. 355–356), which the paper's own dose-dependence finding contradicts; the authors allow that the missing 40% may involve dose dependence (p. 361). The Javaid assay had no internal standard (p. 356).

key_findings.finding: From the oral and intranasal topical mean curves of Van Dyke et al. (1978; 2 mg/kg, n = 4), absorption half-lives were 7.2 minutes (oral, after an assumed 20-minute lag) and 20.4 minutes (intranasal topical), terminal half-lives 58.6 and 73.6 minutes, and relative bioavailability about 0.3 for both against another laboratory's intravenous data, a comparison the authors call questionable.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 358); Table 3 (p. 360); Results and discussion › Pharmacokinetic parameters, 4th and 5th paragraphs (pp. 360–361)
key_findings.note: The 0.3 values are printed in parentheses; converting 2 mg/kg to an absolute dose for this comparison requires a body weight that is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Coca chewing was not studied: reinterpreting Holmstedt et al. (1979), the authors note that the person with the highest levels chewed 4.4 g of leaves containing 21 mg of cocaine (0.34 mg/kg) and reached 149 ng/ml, and project that a 30 g quid would still keep concentrations below 1000 ng/ml, without showing a calculation.

The authors call their findings tentative because the intravenous studies involved few participants and the literature analyses rest on averaged data, and state that resolving the dose dependence requires measuring drug and metabolites in plasma and urine over an extended dose range.

reporting_issues.issue: The assay was calibrated from 2 to 500 ng/ml (p. 354), yet the first values after 100 mg and most values in the first hour after 200 mg exceed 500 ng/ml (up to 3868 ng/ml in Table 1, and 6990 ng/ml in the repeated-dose session, p. 363); no dilution step, upper limit, precision or accuracy is reported. The paper sets aside other laboratories' data for an unestablished quantitative range and for precision data limited to high concentrations (pp. 356–357).
reporting_issues.consequence: The early concentrations, which drive the fitted intercepts, AUC, clearance and initial concentrations, and the accumulation finding, rest on values outside the documented calibration; the standard the paper applies to other laboratories is not met in its own report.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints late concentrations of 0 (X at 240, 300 and 360 minutes; Y at 360 minutes) without a stated limit of quantification, while the fits weight each point by 1/C² (p. 355), which cannot accommodate a zero; how these points were handled is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: X's terminal half-life (40.3 minutes, the shortest) may depend on how its zero values were treated; this cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The coefficients of variation in the text differ from Table 2: for the oral fit the text gives 7% for α where Table 2 gives 20%; for the intranasal topical fit the text gives a range of 34% to 61%, whereas Table 2 includes 68% (for B).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table values are less favourable than the text's, so the oral absorption estimate is less precise than the text says.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean terminal half-lives of Wilkinson et al. (1980) are first given as 75 minutes (oral) and 48 minutes (nasal) and two sentences later as 48 minutes (oral) and 75 minutes (nasal topical).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that these values agree with the authors' own 59 minutes (oral) and 74 minutes (nasal topical) cannot be checked; under the first assignment neither route agrees.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods state that for absorption curves A = −B (p. 355), but Table 2 gives unequal values (intranasal −295 and 276; oral −577 and 307; intranasal topical −428 and 337), so the fitted curves do not pass through zero at the start of absorption.
reporting_issues.consequence: The fits were evidently unconstrained; the AUC values behind the bioavailability figures carry this misfit in addition to the extrapolation noted under the key findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The repeated-dose session in Z (100 mg plus 100 mg 30 minutes later) is not described in the Clinical protocol, which lists only 100 mg and 200 mg sessions (p. 354); its infusion times and sampling schedule are not reported, its values are not tabulated, and the Fig. 5 legend does not identify the symbols.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's evidence for accumulation cannot be checked beyond the three values in the text and readings from the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The threshold in initial concentration (Fig. 4) compares the intercept of the only two-exponential fit (W at 200 mg: A = 2482 and B = 1997 ng/ml in Table 2, whose sum exceeds the first measured value of 3868 ng/ml) with one-exponential intercepts for the other four sessions, one of which (Z at 200 mg: B = 1432 ng/ml) lies far below its first measured value of 2530 ng/ml (Tables 1–2). By the editors' calculation, A + B = 4479 ng/ml, and the measured 5-minute concentrations per mg/kg were 583–648 ng/ml in the three 100 mg sessions and 1088 (Z) and 1315 (W) in the two 200 mg sessions.
reporting_issues.consequence: On measured values the step lies between the 100 mg and the 200 mg sessions, not between 2.3 and 2.9 mg/kg; the threshold and the exponential dependence of initial concentration on dose depend on mixing model types. The measured values do show disproportionately high early concentrations at 200 mg, in two sessions.

reporting_issues.issue: The bioavailability equation (eqn 6) assumes the same clearance at the two doses compared (pp. 355–356), while the paper's main result is that clearance changes with dose.
reporting_issues.consequence: If clearance were lower at the larger intranasal dose (96 mg) than at the 32 mg intravenous dose, the 60% figure would be overestimated; the authors mention dose dependence only as one possible reason for the missing 40% (p. 361).
